transcript.text: theres a funny smell from my oven when its on

Stop using the oven until you know what the smell is.

• Rotten egg / sulfur / gas smell: This may be a gas leak. Turn the oven off if safe, don’t light matches or use electrical switches, open doors/windows, leave the area, and call your gas emergency line or emergency services from outside.
• Burning plastic, melting, or electrical/“fishy” smell: Turn the oven off at the breaker if you can do so safely. Don’t use it again until it’s checked by an appliance technician/electrician.
• Burning food, grease, or smoke smell: Turn it off, let it cool fully, then check for spilled food, grease buildup, foil, plastic packaging, or anything left inside/on top. Clean it before trying again.
• New oven smell: A mild chemical/oily smell can happen during the first few uses as factory residues burn off. Ventilate well and follow the manufacturer’s “first-use” instructions—but it should fade after a couple of heating cycles.

If you feel dizzy, nauseated, get a headache, or a carbon monoxide alarm goes off, get everyone outside and call emergency services. Carbon monoxide has no smell, so make sure you have a working CO alarm, especially with a gas oven.

What does the smell resemble, and is your oven gas or electric?
its electric. smells a bit like hot plastic or something electrical, kind of from behind the cooker rather than inside the oven

Treat that as a possible electrical fault.

1. Turn the oven/cooker off immediately.
2. Switch it off at the cooker isolator switch or circuit breaker if you can do so safely. Do not keep using it to “see if it happens again.”
3. If there is smoke, sparking, crackling, visible scorching, or the smell is getting stronger: leave the area and call the fire service/emergency number.
4. Once fully cool, don’t pull the cooker out or remove panels yourself. The issue could be the supply cable, connection terminal, plug/socket, heating element wiring, or control components behind it.
5. Arrange for a qualified appliance repair technician or electrician to inspect it before using the cooker again.

If it’s plugged into a normal wall socket and the plug/socket feels hot, looks discoloured, or smells burnt, keep that circuit switched off too.

the cooker switch on the wall looks a bit brown at one corner and felt warm. the kitchen lights flickered once when the oven was on, and I heard a crackle from the back once. smell's been getting stronger over 3-4 days. should I turn the switch off?

Yes—stop using it now and isolate the power. Those are warning signs of overheating/loose wiring: browning, warmth, crackling, worsening electrical/plastic smell, and flickering lights.

Because the wall cooker switch itself is warm and discoloured, it may be unsafe to operate. If you can do so without touching the warm/brown switch, turn off the cooker circuit at your consumer unit/fuse box instead (the breaker labelled cooker/oven). If you’re unsure which breaker it is, switch off the main power only if necessary and safe.

• Do not use the oven, hob, cooker switch, or that circuit again.
• Do not pull the cooker out, remove covers, or inspect wiring yourself.
• If there is smoke, sparks, popping/crackling, flames, or the smell continues after power is isolated: get out, close doors behind you if possible, and call the fire service/emergency number.
• Arrange an urgent qualified electrician (and appliance engineer if needed) before restoring power. The switch/cable/terminal connection may need repair or replacement.
• If you rent, report it as an urgent electrical safety issue to the landlord/maintenance line now.

If the switch is currently crackling, very hot, smoking, or sparking, don’t touch it—leave the area and call emergency services.
